ig_tt_text:
There's a tiny piece of radioactive metal on your ceiling — and it's there to save your life.

Most ionization smoke detectors hold a small button of americium-241. Its alpha particles knock electrons off air molecules, so a tiny current flows between two plates. Smoke soaks up the ions, the current drops, and the alarm goes off. Half of that americium will still be there in 432 years.

Sources: U.S. EPA, U.S. NRC. 3D animation.

tt_title: The radioactive metal on your ceiling
yt_desc:
Most ionization smoke detectors contain a tiny button of americium-241 (less than a millionth of a gram). Its alpha particles ionize the air in a small chamber so a tiny current flows between two plates. When smoke drifts in, it binds the ions, the current drops and the alarm sounds. Americium-241 has a half-life of about 432 years.

Sources:
- U.S. EPA, 'Radioactivity in Antiques / Smoke Detectors' (epa.gov/radtown)
- U.S. Nuclear Regulatory Commission, Smoke Detectors backgrounder
